newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanian industrialists seek more Iraqi business.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian industrialists seek more Iraqi business.

text.p: Leading Jordanian industrialists said on Thursday they would lobby their government to raise by $50 million a trade protocol with Iraq to accelerate a growth in exports since Baghdad's U.N. oil-for-food deal.

Khaldoun Abu Hassan, head of the Amman Chamber of Commerce which is leading the campaign to improve links with Iraq said a recent meeting in Baghdad with top Iraqi officials discussed expanding a $220 million annual protocol which barters Jordanian goods for Iraqi oil.
Jordan depends on Iraq for all its energy needs.

"We are seeking to raise this year's protocol by an extra $50 million to cater for as many industries as possible which do not presently export under the protocol," he told Reuters. New exporters could be limited to contracts worth $500,000 each to widen the benefits as much as possible, he added.
The government wants to improve political ties with Iraq to help it benefit from a U.N. deal which allows Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food and medicine.

But it has resisted pressure from both its industrialist lobby and Iraq to raise the protocol, which is exempt from tough U.N. sanctions imposed on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait. Protocol deals are tightly controlled by the government which handles exporter payments under an escrow account from revenues of the oil sales.
Jordan halved the value of the protocol in 1996 to just $220 million at a time when political relations had plummeted.
Despite the sanctions, Iraq remains Jordan's biggest trading partner and has kept up supplies of oil at nearly half world prices.

Abu Hassan's team told Iraqi officials including Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz they would push their government to seek U.N. sanction exemptions on imports of Iraq's competitively priced urea and sulphur.
Jordan has stopped commercial imports of any goods from Iraq since tighter U.N. inspections on the border in 1992. It no longer buys dates, which Jordanians say are now purchased from Dubai.

Jordan's Chamber of Industry also plans to push the government to question more aggressively the delay in approving most of the $130 million worth of deals won under the U.N. oil-for-food deal -- covering a range of goods from detergents, soaps and vegetable ghee to medicines.
Businessmen say a delay of over five months in approving awards has eroded gains which initially put Jordan second among the league of countries awarded "oil-for-food" deals.
They say delays in approvals as the first six-months U.N. deal comes to an end may cost them dearly in raw materials and lost capacity.

"If it continues it will hurt because many firms have planned their production schedule..," said Issam al-Saket, managing director of Arab Pharmaceutical Manufacturing, which waited five months to win approvals for just seven out of 25 contracts it won in December and January.
The other 18 approvals are still pending, he said.
The firm is one of three major drug firms with a lion's share of $30-40 million worth of deals to Iraq.
Many businessmen complain bitterly that approvals from the U.N. sanction committee are not only painstakingly slow but are biased against Jordan over its special ties with Baghdad.

"We do not know why Jordanian companies appear to be firms which have had the biggest share of suspended contracts..the U.N. committee is penalising Jordan more than Iraq," said Abdul-Noor Habaybeh head of Jordan Paper and Cardboard Company.
